column1: # mapping_set_description: Related Agentic Skill Risks stated in each section of the OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 whitepaper V1. Each comment is the whitepaper's own explanation of the relationship; both directions are recorded where the whitepaper states both.

column9: comment
Often the delivery mechanism for malicious skills.
Malicious skills exploit excessive permissions, including logic-layer injection of privileged actions (LPCI).
Brand impersonation enables malicious skill distribution.
A malicious author can hide the payload in referenced external content, keeping the skill body clean.
Ineffective detection allows malicious skills to proliferate.
Identity artifacts cloned or ported across platforms lose their original protections, aiding impersonation.
Supply chain compromise enables delivery of malicious skills.
Externally referenced documentation is a supply-chain surface that code-integrity controls cannot pin or verify.
Lack of immutable updates exacerbates supply chain risks.
Inadequate scanning misses supply chain vulnerabilities.
Inconsistent security across platforms creates supply chain gaps.
Over-privileged skills amplify the impact of malicious payloads by providing broader access vectors.
Compromised registries may distribute skills with inflated permission requests.
Misleading permission declarations in manifests can hide over-privileged access.
Host-mode execution removes permission boundaries entirely.
Lack of permission review processes allows over-privileged skills to proliferate.
Insecure metadata enables social engineering, and unsafe parsing executes malicious payloads.
Metadata spoofing and serialized exploits hide supply-chain attacks.
Misleading permission declarations grant excessive access.
AST04 executes payloads from the skill's own files; AST05 covers instructions loaded from externally referenced documents.
Host-mode execution amplifies the impact of deserialization code execution.
Metadata and deserialization attacks both evade pattern-matching scanners.
A malicious author can place the payload in referenced content rather than the skill body, so the skill itself stays clean and passes inspection.
AST02 covers the code and dependency supply chain, which integrity controls can pin and verify; AST05 covers the documentation a skill points to, which those controls do not reach.
AST04 executes a payload through unsafe parsing of the skill's own files at load time; AST05 requires no code execution - the agent simply follows instructions in externally referenced text.
AST07 addresses the skill version changing; AST05 is the same drift applied to referenced content, which can change while the skill stays pinned and unchanged.
Externally referenced content can be absent at scan time or served selectively, widening AST08's detection gap to content a scanner may never see.
Weak isolation allows malicious skills to escape sandboxes and access host resources.
Compromised skills can exploit isolation weaknesses to persist.
Host-mode execution bypasses permission controls entirely.
Isolation failures can lead to code execution from deserialized data.
Lack of isolation enforcement enables shadow deployments.
Update drift can introduce malicious code through compromised updates.
Unverified updates are a supply chain attack vector.
Update metadata may be spoofed to hide malicious changes.
Referenced external content can drift maliciously with no version change to the pinned skill.
Updated skills may not be re-scanned, allowing new vulnerabilities.
Lack of update policies enables uncontrolled drift.
Poor scanning allows malicious skills to pass undetected.
Compromised skills may evade scanners.
Metadata and deserialization attacks can bypass static-analysis and pattern-matching scanners.
Externally referenced content may be absent or cloaked at scan time, evading scanners entirely.
Updated skills may not be re-scanned.
Governance gaps allow malicious skills to be deployed without oversight.
Lack of governance enables supply chain attacks.
No review processes allow excessive permissions.
Governance failures lead to shadow deployments.
Lack of governance allows uncontrolled updates.
Cross-platform reuse allows malicious skills to spread across ecosystems.
Compromised skills can be reused across platforms.
Inconsistent metadata formats create confusion and exploitation.
Skills may pass scanning on one platform but be vulnerable on another.
Lack of cross-platform governance enables skill proliferation.
